title: Effects of illuminance and correlated color temperature on emotional responses and lighting adjustment behaviors

findings.antecedent: initial illuminance level (45-290 lx vs 420-780 lx)
findings.mechanism: Lower brightness is associated with greater pleasure, aligning with previous findings on comfort under lower light levels.
findings.quote: greater pleasure was associated with lower brightness (45-290lx) compared to higher brightness (420–780lx)

findings.mechanism: Higher CCT (blue light) was reported as a higher level of pleasure in comparison with a lower CCT (red-yellow light).
findings.quote: the reverse trend was observed for CCT

findings.antecedent: initial illuminance level (45-290 lx vs 420-780 lx)
findings.mechanism: Higher brightness is associated with heightened alertness and arousal, supported by circadian rhythm influence and physiological activity.
findings.quote: participants rated their level of arousal higher in higher brightness (i.e., 45-290lx vs. 420-780lx)

findings.mechanism: The higher CCT did not result in significantly higher arousal, suggesting CCT's effect on arousal is less pronounced than illuminance.
findings.quote: the higher CCT did not result in significantly higher arousal

findings.mechanism: Women showed larger and more consistent reactions to illuminance, with brighter lighting associated with reduced emotional valence.
findings.quote: women showed larger and more consistent reactions to illuminance, with brighter lighting associated with reduced emotional valence

findings.antecedent: gender x initial correlated color temperature (CCT)
findings.mechanism: Men showed a slightly stronger reaction pattern than women, feeling more positive about high CCTs and less positive about low CCTs.
findings.quote: men showed a slightly stronger reaction pattern than women.

findings.mechanism: Women showed larger and more consistent reactions to illuminance, with brighter lighting associated with reduced emotional valence.
findings.quote: women showed larger and more consistent reactions to illuminance, with brighter lighting associated with reduced emotional valence

findings.antecedent: gender x initial correlated color temperature (CCT)
findings.mechanism: Men showed a stronger response to low CCTs than to medium and high, whereas women's arousal did not differ much across different CCTs.
findings.quote: men showed a stronger response to low CCTs than to medium and high, whereas women's arousal did not differ much across different CCTs.

findings.mechanism: Females displayed a greater change in arousal levels than males with increased illuminance.

findings.mechanism: Anchor effect: participants' adjustments are made to align with the initial conditions, indicating that starting conditions significantly impact subsequent preferences.
findings.quote: there was a significant main effect of initial illuminance on adjusted illuminance

findings.antecedent: gender x initial correlated color temperature (CCT)
findings.mechanism: Women adjusted CCT to lower values compared to men, indicating gender-specific preferences.
findings.quote: The difference in coefficients between genders (Women - Men) was 0.07, SE = 0.03, 95% CI: [-0.13, -0.02].

findings.mechanism: Women adjusted illuminance to lower values compared to men, indicating gender-specific preferences.
findings.quote: The difference in coefficients between genders (Women – Men) was -0.12, SE = 0.04, 95% CI: [0.20, -0.04].

findings.antecedent: order of lighting conditions presented (greater number of prior conditions)
findings.mechanism: Participant adaptation to the VR display, increased light sensitivity, or fatigue may lead to a preference for less arousing light conditions over time.
findings.quote: Both men and women adjusted significantly lower values for the lighting intensity... after experiencing a greater number of prior conditions

findings.antecedent: order of lighting conditions presented (greater number of prior conditions)
findings.mechanism: Participant adaptation to the VR display, increased light sensitivity, or fatigue may lead to a preference for less arousing light conditions over time.
findings.quote: marginally significantly lower CCTs after experiencing a greater number of prior conditions

findings.consequent: illuminance adjustment uncertainty (number of button presses against preferred direction)
findings.mechanism: Lower illuminance values were associated with greater uncertainty, suggesting more hesitation in user actions.
findings.quote: Higher lumen levels led to lower lumen uncertainty, with a coefficient of -0.11, SE = 0.01, 95% CI: [−0.13, -0.08].

findings.consequent: CCT adjustment uncertainty (number of button presses against preferred direction)
findings.mechanism: Mid-range CCT values were associated with the greatest Adjustment Uncertainty, but the main effect of initial CCT was not significant.
findings.quote: As for CCT uncertainty, we found a significant gender main effect and significant gender by initial CCT interaction effect.

limitations: Current VR systems do not provide a full dynamic range compared to real-world lighting, limiting generalizability to real-world contexts.
Findings might differ between studies using different game engines or tone mapping algorithms.
Limited sample size and convenient recruitment method (Cornell University students/faculty) limit generalizability to diverse populations.
Loss of data from multiple participants due to technical glitches impacted sample size, though not biased.
